results.corrected_title: Reuters: Hacker used autonomous AI agents to break into websites of more than 100 companies
results.corrected_summary: Reuters reported on 19 October that a Chinese-speaking hacker used Cairn, an open-source AI tool, to send AI agents at more than 1,200 e-commerce websites in the US, Canada, Australia and Japan. Websites belonging to more than 100 companies were breached, including sites linked to Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at NorForge, found the campaign and estimated it used about 5,000 dollars in tokens, roughly 50 dollars per successful hack. A worker label pointed to DeepSeek run through Claude Code, but the models were not independently verified.
key_facts: Cairn is an open-source AI tool built for authorized penetration testing; its author ('le1xia0') said it was not designed for attacks
More than 1,200 sites targeted and more than 100 companies' websites breached
Named companies: Deere (no sign sensitive data was accessed), SharkNinja (only a standalone product support site was hit) and Cummins
About 5,000 dollars in tokens, roughly 50 dollars per successful hack (Fagerland/NorForge estimate)
NorForge found about two dozen malicious Cairn instances, active from around 2 October
results.issues: Mostly accurate. The claim that it 'appeared to use DeepSeek and Claude Code' is uncertain: The Hacker News says only a worker label ('claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash') suggests this, and neither Reuters nor the researcher verified it. The breached sites were partly peripheral, for example SharkNinja's standalone support site, and Deere saw no sign that sensitive data was accessed.

results.corrected_title: Texas sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over ChatGPT safety claims and child protection
results.corrected_summary: On 23 October Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman in Collin County district court, alleging deceptive marketing of ChatGPT's safety, accuracy and reliability under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The suit also says ChatGPT broke the SCOPE Act by lacking required age verification for minors. Texas wants Altman held personally liable and seeks civil penalties reported at 10,000 dollars per violation, surrender of profits, and an injunction blocking minors from ChatGPT and requiring a court-appointed evaluator to approve new models. The suit is separate from the lawsuits eight other states announced on 14 October.
key_facts: Filed on Friday 23 October 2026 in Collin County district court
Claims under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the SCOPE Act (age verification)
Seeks to hold Sam Altman personally liable
Seeks an injunction blocking minors from ChatGPT and court-appointed evaluator approval of new models
Eight states (Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Montana) announced separate suits on 14 October

other_sources.name: Texas AG press release via EIN Presswire

results.issues: The Houston Chronicle page would not load. The 10,000 dollars per violation and profit disgorgement come only from search-result summaries, not from an article I opened, and one outlet reportedly cited 'over 1 million dollars' in monetary relief. 'Failure to warn' is a quote from Paxton, not a confirmed separate count. The eight-state suits on 14 October are confirmed by multiple outlets.

results.corrected_title: Goldman Sachs: AI job losses may show up mainly in downturns
results.corrected_summary: A Goldman Sachs note by economist Joseph Briggs, published 22 October, finds that labor disruption from automation is limited in healthy economies but speeds up during cyclical slowdowns. The note repeats that if AI lifts productivity by 15 percent in developed economies, up to 9 percent of workers could be displaced, with slower hiring cutting employment by another 3 percent. Historically, each 1 percent gain in technology-driven productivity raised the cumulative gross job-loss rate by 0.5-0.6 points. Only 23 percent of US establishments have built AI into regular workflows.
key_facts: Goldman note by Joseph Briggs published 22 October 2026
Up to 9% displacement plus a 3% drag from slower hiring, assuming a 15% productivity lift
Each 1% of tech-driven productivity gain historically raised cumulative gross job loss by 0.5-0.6 points
Automation-driven labor disruption accelerates during cyclical slowdowns
23% of US establishments have AI in regular workflows
August 2025 estimate was 6-7% (range 3-14%); about 9% (around 15 million workers over a decade) already by June 2026
results.issues: The 9% figure is not new. Fortune itself says Briggs put it at about 9% (around 15 million workers) by June 2026, so the idea that Goldman just raised its estimate from 6-7% is misleading. The genuinely new part is the 22 October note's finding that layoffs accelerate in downturns, and the headline should focus on that. Only one source (Fortune) confirms the October note. I did not open the PYMNTS page; it appeared in search results and covers the earlier mid-2026 9% estimate, not the October note.
